# Welcome {.unnumbered}

This is the course book for **DATS 2102 — Data Visualization for Data Science**, an undergraduate course at the George Washington University.

The course introduces the principles and practice of data visualization with Python. Across twelve weeks you'll move from environment setup and the grammar of graphics through distributions, wrangling, perception, comparison, annotation, mapping, color, modeling, uncertainty, and visualization for machine learning — building practical skills on real datasets along the way.

## How this book works

Each chapter corresponds to one week of the course, with two 75-minute sessions (a theory-focused **Session 1** and a hands-on **Session 2**). Within a chapter you'll find background and motivation, learning objectives, readings, a setup checklist, the session outline, code snippets, an in-class activity, homework, and a submission checklist.

A note on the code in this book:

- Most code snippets are **executable** — the charts you see were produced by running the code when the book was rendered. Many use datasets that ship with `seaborn` or `plotly` (loaded at render time).
- A few snippets depend on **local data files** or external resources and are shown as **copy-and-run source** rather than executed (for example, parts of the mapping week). Each week's full **hands-on notebook and data** are available as **downloads**, linked from within the chapter.

## Course arc

- **Weeks 1–4 — Foundations.** Getting started, the language of graphs, distributions and variation, and wrangling with pandas.
- **Weeks 5–7 — Design & comparison.** Perception and principles, comparisons, and text/labels/tables.
- **Weeks 8–12 — Maps, color & models.** Mapping, color and accessibility, relationships and modeling, uncertainty, and visualization for ML/NLP.
- **Projects.** A mid-term project and a final project.

## Working with the notebooks

The hands-on material for each week lives in downloadable Jupyter notebooks (and their data), linked inside the relevant chapter. Submit your work by rendering your notebook to HTML with Quarto and uploading to Blackboard, as described in each week's submission checklist.
